title.en: How many arbitrators should decide the dispute?

tooltip.en: Sets how many arbitrators decide the dispute. The choice drives cost, speed and how the tribunal is appointed.

questions.tooltip_status: signoff_required (spec paragraph 8 item 3: EN draft by intern, 04.08.2026, for owner correction rather than drafting; deliberately number-free: no article numbers, no thresholds, no rules-version references)

explanation.en: One arbitrator is faster and cheaper, and is the usual choice for ordinary commercial disputes. Three arbitrators cost more and take longer to appoint, but each side gets a hand in shaping the tribunal and no single person carries the decision alone, which parties often prefer for high-value or complex disputes. Leaving the choice to the ICC Court is not a gap in the clause: the Court then fixes the number based on the circumstances of the case.

title.en: How should the president of the tribunal be selected?

tooltip.en: Decides who nominates the president of a three-member tribunal: the two co-arbitrators together, or the ICC Court.

questions.tooltip_status: signoff_required (spec paragraph 8 item 3: EN draft by intern, 04.08.2026, for owner correction rather than drafting; deliberately number-free: no article numbers, no thresholds, no rules-version references. Review together with f_president, itself signoff_required.)

explanation.en: With a joint nomination, the arbitrators chosen by each side agree on the chair, which gives the parties indirect influence over the tribunal's composition and is common in practice. If the co-arbitrators cannot agree, or if you prefer neutrality by design, the ICC Court appoints the president under its standard procedure. Choosing the Court is not a downgrade; it is the default mechanism the Rules provide.

title.en: What should be the place of arbitration?

tooltip.en: The seat is the legal home of the arbitration, not just a venue: it determines which courts supervise the proceedings and where the award is legally made.

questions.tooltip_status: signoff_required (spec paragraph 8 item 3: EN draft by intern, 04.08.2026, for owner correction rather than drafting; deliberately number-free: no article numbers, no thresholds, no rules-version references)

explanation.en: The seat fixes the procedural law of the arbitration, decides which national courts can assist or intervene, and shapes how the resulting award travels internationally. Hearings can still take place elsewhere, or online: the seat is a legal anchor, not a promise to meet there. Established arbitration seats offer predictable, arbitration-friendly courts; if the parties cannot agree on one, leaving the seat to the ICC Court keeps the clause workable.

title.en: What should be the language of arbitration?

tooltip.en: Fixes the language of the proceedings: submissions, hearings and the award.

questions.tooltip_status: signoff_required (spec paragraph 8 item 3: EN draft by intern, 04.08.2026, for owner correction rather than drafting; deliberately number-free: no article numbers, no thresholds, no rules-version references)

explanation.en: The practical rule is to pick the language of the contract and of most of the likely evidence, because translating documents and testimony is a real cost driver. A single language keeps the procedure efficient, and the tribunal can order translations where needed. If the parties work in different languages and cannot agree, leaving the choice to the tribunal avoids turning the clause negotiation into a stalemate.

title.en: Do you want to determine the law applicable to the arbitration agreement?

tooltip.en: Chooses the law governing the arbitration agreement itself, which can differ from the law of the main contract.

questions.tooltip_status: signoff_required (spec paragraph 8 item 3: EN draft by intern, 04.08.2026, for owner correction rather than drafting; deliberately number-free: no article numbers, no thresholds, no rules-version references. Review together with f_gov_law, itself signoff_required.)

explanation.en: The arbitration agreement is legally separable from the contract around it, so its validity and scope can be judged under a law of its own. If the clause says nothing, courts in different countries answer that question differently, which invites side disputes exactly when the clause is under attack. Naming the law costs one sentence and removes that uncertainty; parties commonly align it with the law of the seat or the law of the main contract.

title.en: Should the arbitration be confidential?

tooltip.en: Decides whether the parties expressly commit to keeping the arbitration confidential.

questions.tooltip_status: signoff_required (spec paragraph 8 item 3: EN draft by intern, 04.08.2026, for owner correction rather than drafting; deliberately number-free: no article numbers, no thresholds, no rules-version references. Review together with f_confidentiality, itself signoff_required. Replaces the wireframe placeholder kept since v0.1.)

explanation.en: Arbitration hearings are private, but privacy is not confidentiality: the ICC Rules do not impose a general confidentiality obligation on the parties themselves. If confidentiality matters, the clause must say so; if it stays silent, protection depends on the law of the seat and may be thinner than expected. An express duty also has consequences of its own, for example when a dispute must be disclosed to insurers, auditors or regulators, so some parties deliberately leave it out.

title.en: Do you want to modify the Emergency Arbitrator Provisions?

tooltip.en: Controls access to an emergency arbitrator for urgent measures before the tribunal exists.

questions.tooltip_status: signoff_required (spec paragraph 8 item 3: EN draft by intern, 04.08.2026, for owner correction rather than drafting; deliberately number-free: no article numbers, no thresholds, no rules-version references)

explanation.en: By default, a party can ask an emergency arbitrator for urgent interim relief in the window before the tribunal is constituted, for example to stop an asset from disappearing or evidence from being destroyed. Opting out closes that door; urgent relief then comes from the state courts alone, which some parties prefer where local injunctions are fast and reliable. Keeping the default adds nothing to the clause text; it simply preserves the option for whichever party one day needs speed.

title.en: Do you want to modify the Expedited Proceedings Provisions?

tooltip.en: Adjusts whether the ICC's fast-track procedure applies. By default it covers disputes below a ceiling set by the Rules.

questions.tooltip_status: signoff_required (spec paragraph 8 item 3: EN draft by intern, 04.08.2026, for owner correction rather than drafting; deliberately number-free: no article numbers, no thresholds, no rules-version references)

explanation.en: The expedited procedure trades procedural room for speed and lower cost, and by default it applies automatically below the ceiling the ICC Rules set from time to time. You can extend it to disputes of any size, set your own ceiling, or exclude it entirely if you want the full procedure regardless of amount. One interaction to weigh: under the expedited framework the ICC Court may put the case before a sole arbitrator even where the clause provides for three, so this answer works together with your choice on the number of arbitrators.

title.en: Do you want to explicitly grant the arbitral tribunal the power to limit document production requests?

tooltip.en: Decides whether the clause expressly empowers the tribunal to keep document production within limits.

questions.tooltip_status: signoff_required (spec paragraph 8 item 3: EN draft by intern, 04.08.2026, for owner correction rather than drafting; deliberately number-free: no article numbers, no thresholds, no rules-version references)

explanation.en: Document production is one of the main cost drivers in arbitration, and expectations differ sharply between legal traditions. An express power to limit production signals from the outset that the tribunal can keep requests proportionate, which helps when a party comes from a discovery-heavy background. Tribunals generally hold broad case-management powers anyway, so this sentence is less about creating a power than about removing the argument over it.

title.en: Are there other contracts that form part of the same transaction or are closely related to this contract?

tooltip.en: Flags whether this contract belongs to a wider set of agreements whose dispute clauses should work together.

questions.tooltip_status: signoff_required (spec paragraph 8 item 3: EN draft by intern, 04.08.2026, for owner correction rather than drafting; deliberately number-free: no article numbers, no thresholds, no rules-version references)

explanation.en: When related contracts carry different dispute resolution clauses, one commercial conflict can splinter into parallel proceedings with inconsistent outcomes. This question therefore produces guidance rather than clause text: if related contracts exist, the practical task is to keep their clauses consistent, and that is a review of the whole contract set rather than of a single clause. Your answer does not change the generated wording; it changes what you should check before signing.

title.en: Do you anticipate including parties who have not signed the main contract in potential arbitration proceedings (e.g., affiliates, guarantors)?

tooltip.en: Flags whether parties who never signed the contract, such as affiliates or guarantors, may need to join a future arbitration.

questions.tooltip_status: signoff_required (spec paragraph 8 item 3: EN draft by intern, 04.08.2026, for owner correction rather than drafting; deliberately number-free: no article numbers, no thresholds, no rules-version references)

explanation.en: Arbitration binds those who agreed to it, so bringing in non-signatories is legally delicate and depends heavily on the facts and the applicable law. If affiliates, guarantors or other group companies may end up in the dispute, the reliable route is tailored drafting across all the relevant documents, not a standard clause. Like the related-contracts question, this one produces a warning instead of text: its job is to tell you when a standard clause stops being enough.

title.en: Would you like to add mediation provisions to your arbitration clause?

tooltip.en: Adds a mediation layer to the clause, so the parties try a settlement track before or alongside arbitration.

questions.tooltip_status: signoff_required (spec paragraph 8 item 3: EN draft by intern, 04.08.2026, for owner correction rather than drafting; deliberately number-free: no article numbers, no thresholds, no rules-version references)

explanation.en: Mediation is a structured negotiation guided by a neutral, and settling there is usually far cheaper than fighting an arbitration to the end. Written into the clause, it can range from a gentle option to a mandatory step before arbitration can start, depending on the variant chosen next. The design question is bite: more obligation creates more settlement pressure, but the strictest form also delays access to the tribunal, which matters if your disputes tend to be urgent.

title.en: What type of mediation provision would you prefer?

tooltip.en: Chooses how strongly the clause commits the parties to mediation, from purely optional to a mandatory step before arbitration.

questions.tooltip_status: signoff_required (spec paragraph 8 item 3: EN draft by intern, 04.08.2026, for owner correction rather than drafting; deliberately number-free: no article numbers, no thresholds, no rules-version references. Review together with the four mediation fragments, themselves signoff_required.)

explanation.en: The variants differ in the obligation they create. Variant A keeps mediation available at any time without restraining arbitration; Variant B obliges the parties to consider mediation first; Variant C requires starting mediation but lets arbitration proceed in parallel; Variant D makes mediation a true precondition, so arbitration must wait out an agreed period. The stricter the variant, the stronger the settlement pressure and the later a tribunal can act, so match it to how urgent your disputes are likely to be.

title.en: How long should parties wait after initiating mediation before being allowed to commence arbitration?

tooltip.en: Sets how long arbitration must wait after mediation begins. It exists only where mediation is a mandatory first step.

questions.tooltip_status: signoff_required (spec paragraph 8 item 3: EN draft by intern, 04.08.2026, for owner correction rather than drafting; deliberately number-free: no article numbers, no thresholds, no rules-version references)

explanation.en: This period gives mediation a protected window: arbitration on the same dispute must wait until the period runs out or the parties settle. A shorter period keeps pressure on and preserves quick access to the tribunal; a longer one gives settlement more room but delays enforcement of your rights. The recommended default balances the two, and unless the clause opts out of emergency arbitration, urgent interim measures stay available during the wait.

assembly.framing: Header, then an empty line, then the clause text (§5.1). The clause body is a single paragraph unless a mediation variant requires a second one. Mediation provisions carry no internal heading.
assembly.order_rule: in_clause fragments assemble by ascending order into ONE paragraph (§5.2): base 10, president 20, seat 30, language 40, governing law 50, confidentiality 60, EA opt-out 70, expedited 80, three-arb override 85, document production 90. A replaces_base fragment displaces f_base and heads that same paragraph, absorbing the in_clause sentences after it (§5.3 Variant D). paragraph_before fragments render before the clause paragraph (Variants B, C); paragraph_after fragments render after it (Variant A).
assembly.completeness_gate: The clause is presented as final (review screen, final screen, copy) only once every currently visible question is answered; no fragment may be emitted with an unfilled mandatory slot (§7.1).
assembly.hidden_answer_rule: Answers of questions hidden by a later change leave the output but are retained; they are restored if the question becomes visible again (§7.1).

features.live_preview: Updates on each selection, before moving on; visible update is a segment-level edit (§7.2, visual requirement; internally full recompute + diff is fine).

q.en: Which arbitration rules does this tool use?

a.en: Currently, it generates agreements based on the Rules of Arbitration of the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC).
No. It's an automated tool for informational purposes only and does not replace tailored legal counsel.
Businesses and individuals needing a straightforward ICC arbitration clause. Use "Simple Version" for basic needs or "Advanced Mode" for more options, but always consider seeking legal advice.

a.en: The tool provides standard wording. For it to be binding, it must be correctly incorporated into a valid contract under the applicable law. Review by legal counsel is recommended.

q.en: What about other rules (VIAC, DIS) or highly custom clauses?

a.en: This builder is currently ICC-focused. For other rules or bespoke needs, please contact us for tailored advice.

q.en: What happens to my entered information?

a.en: The tool uses selections in real-time only. We don't permanently store the specific details entered. See our Privacy Policy for general site data practices.

items.status: signoff_required (C.7 point 2: should also state nothing reaches the firm unless the enquiry form is submitted, §7.9)

q.en: What if I'm unsure about an option?

a.en: Choosing options like the number of arbitrators or the seat has significant legal and cost implications. If unsure, seek professional legal advice before finalizing your agreement.

site_policies.analytics: Funnel milestones only, no content, no session linkage (§7.8, decided 30.07.2026). Site-level; nothing to build in the static builder page itself. Standing README constraint.
site_policies.enquiry_prefill: Enquiry form carries the built clause in a visible, editable, clearly labelled field; only clause text, never answers or mode (§7.9, decided 30.07.2026). Site-level.
site_policies.privacy_structure: Builder page fully static: no runtime database call, no visitor input leaving the browser (§1.3/§1.4).
